items.item: The Master theorem solves T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) with constants a >= 1, b > 1 and f asymptotically positive, by comparing f(n) with the watershed function n^(log_b a), which is exactly the number of leaves a^(log_b n) of the recursion tree.

at.step: The statement: f against the watershed

items.item: Recursion-tree picture of the three cases: level i costs a^i f(n/b^i). The level sums form a geometric series that is dominated by the root (the f-heavy case), even across all levels (the balanced case, Θ(f · log n)), or dominated by the leaves (the leaf-heavy case, Θ(n^(log_b a))). This is the picture to animate.
Case 1 (leaf-dominated) needs f(n) = O(n^(log_b a − ε)) for some ε > 0, which means polynomially smaller. Being merely little-o of n^(log_b a) is not enough.

at.step: The statement: f against the watershed

items.item: Case 2 (balanced) in its extended form: if f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · lg^k n) with k >= 0, then T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · lg^(k+1) n). The basic k = 0 case gives the familiar extra log factor.

Case 3 (root-dominated) needs two things: f(n) = Ω(n^(log_b a + ε)), and the regularity condition a·f(n/b) <= c·f(n) for some constant c < 1 and all sufficiently large n. Regularity is what makes the level sums decrease geometrically. Some lecture statements drop the c < 1 requirement, and they are wrong to.

at.step: The statement: f against the watershed

items.item: The three cases are not exhaustive. There are gaps where f is larger or smaller than n^(log_b a) only by a sub-polynomial factor. Example: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n lg n is not covered by the basic statement, but it is covered by extended Case 2 or by Akra–Bazzi, and equals Θ(n lg^2 n).

Floors and ceilings in subproblem sizes, such as T(⌈n/2⌉) + T(⌊n/2⌋), do not change the asymptotic solution of a divide-and-conquer recurrence. An expert knows why this holds, not just that it holds: either a perturbation term in the theorem (Akra–Bazzi's h_i) or monotone sandwiching between powers of b.

Domain transformation to remove floors, ceilings and additive shifts: overestimate T(n) <= 2T(n/2 + 1) + n, then set S(n) = T(n + α), choosing α (here α = 2) so that S satisfies a clean Master-form recurrence.

Change of variables: substitute n = 2^k (t(k) = T(2^k)) to turn a recurrence with an awkward shape into a familiar one. For example, T(n) = T(n/2) + T(n/4) + 1 becomes a Fibonacci-like linear recurrence, giving Θ(n^(lg φ)). The same trick (m = lg n) handles recurrences such as T(n) = 2T(√n) + lg n.

at.deep: Change of variables: the van Emde Boas recurrence

items.item: Some divide-and-conquer recurrences fit neither the Master theorem nor Akra–Bazzi, because the number or size of subproblems is not a constant fraction. Example: T(n) = √n·T(√n) + n has depth lg lg n, with every level summing to n, so T(n) = Θ(n lg lg n). Use a recursion tree or substitution for these.

Unbalanced recursion trees (unequal splits) can be bounded by full levels. Every complete level sums to the same amount (or decays geometrically), and leaves lie between the shallowest depth log_{1/b_min} n and the deepest depth log_{1/b_max} n. Extending the tree to the deepest leaf gives an upper bound, and truncating at the shallowest leaf gives a lower bound.

items.item: A recursion tree that sums '...' is a way to generate a guess, not a proof. The rigorous step is to verify the guess by induction (substitution), or to cite a theorem whose hypotheses you have checked.

at.step: Predict: the proof that proves nothing

items.item: Substitution-method pitfall: you must prove exactly the induction hypothesis T(n) <= cn with the same constant c. Getting T(n) <= cn + n and calling it 'O(n)' is invalid, because the constant drifts at every level. You cannot induct over big-O.

at.step: Predict: the proof that proves nothing

items.item: When a correct guess fails by a lower-order term, strengthen the hypothesis by subtracting one. Example: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n fails with T(n) <= c·n^2 but succeeds with T(n) <= c1·n^2 − c2·n. A stronger hypothesis is easier to push through the induction.

at.step: The right guess that fails, and the fix

items.item: Base cases in substitution proofs: the base case of the induction is not the base case of the recurrence. Choose n0 and verify enough small values (for example n = 2, 3 when T(1) <= c·1·lg 1 = 0 fails), and choose the constants large enough to cover them. For divide-and-conquer recurrences the boundary values do not affect the asymptotic answer, except in degenerate cases such as T(n) = 2T(n/2) with T(1) = 0.

at.deep: A recurrence is a program's step count

items.item: Substitution only checks a guess and cannot show it is tight. If an upper-bound induction goes through for every constant, however small, the bound is probably loose. Prove a matching lower bound, or tighten the guess, as in moving from n lg n to n lg lg n for √n·T(√n) + n.

Akra–Bazzi statement: for T(x) = Σ_{i=1..k} a_i T(b_i x + h_i(x)) + g(x) with constants a_i > 0 and 0 < b_i < 1, let p be the unique real with Σ a_i b_i^p = 1. Then T(x) = Θ(x^p (1 + ∫_1^x g(u)/u^(p+1) du)). Unlike the Master theorem, it handles unequal splits, non-integer a_i, and p <= 0.

Akra–Bazzi needs a growth condition on g: |g'(x)| bounded by a polynomial (Lehman–Leighton–Meyer), or Leighton's polynomial-growth condition that g(u) is within constant factors of g(x) for u in [b_i x, x]. Polynomially bounded functions such as x^2 log x qualify. An exponential g = 2^n does not, and then T = Θ(g) instead.

The h_i(x) perturbation terms in Akra–Bazzi absorb floors, ceilings and small shifts of subproblem sizes, provided |h_i(x)| = O(x / log^2 x). Leighton's version allows x / log^(1+ε) x and notes that this bound is nearly tight. That fact justifies dropping ⌊ ⌋ and ⌈ ⌉ in the analysis.

Finding p: the function φ(p) = Σ a_i b_i^p is strictly decreasing in p, so p is unique. You often do not need its closed form, only which side of a threshold it lies on. If Σ a_i b_i < 1 then p < 1, and with g(n) = n the integral is Θ(n^(1−p)), so T(n) = Θ(n). If the value of p is needed, solve numerically (p ≈ 0.83978 for selection).

The Master theorem is a special case of Akra–Bazzi (k = 1 gives p = log_b a, and the integral reproduces the three cases and their gaps). When in doubt, compute the Akra–Bazzi integral rather than forcing a Master case.

The selection (median-of-medians) recurrence T(n) <= T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + O(n) is linear because the subproblem fractions sum to 9/10 < 1. Each level of the recursion tree does at most 9/10 of the work of the level above, so the series is geometric. This is the canonical unequal-split example for Akra–Bazzi.

at.step: An unequal split: the lopsided tree

items.item: Why the group size is 5: with groups of 3 the recurrence becomes T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + O(n). The fractions sum to exactly 1, so every level costs n over Θ(log n) levels and T(n) = Θ(n log n). The boundary case Σ fractions = 1 gives the extra log factor, and Σ < 1 is what gives linear time.

Original source of linear-time selection: BFPRT (1973) prove that PICK makes at most 5.4305n comparisons. Linearity follows because each pass discards a constant fraction at a cost proportional to what it discards, and the column length must be at least 5.

at.quote: deterministic BFPRT with groups of five

items.item: Master-theorem instances that experts recognise immediately: Karatsuba (a = 3, b = 2, f = Θ(n) gives Θ(n^(lg 3)) ≈ n^1.585) and Strassen (a = 7, b = 2, f = Θ(n^2) gives Θ(n^(lg 7)) ≈ n^2.81). Both are leaf-dominated, so lowering a matters more than lowering f.

at.step: The statement: f against the watershed

items.item: Full-history recurrences, such as expected randomized-quicksort cost T(n) = (2/n) Σ_{k<n} T(k) + n, are not divide-and-conquer recurrences. Neither the Master theorem nor Akra–Bazzi applies. Solve them by differencing to a limited-history recurrence, or analyse them with indicator variables.

Beyond Θ: the exact solution of the discrete recurrence (with real floors and ceilings) can oscillate. Typically T(n) ~ Ψ(log n)·n^p with Ψ periodic when the log b_i are rationally related, as in mergesort's comparison count. Master theorem and Akra–Bazzi give only the order of growth, not the leading constant.
